III-11.explain: Cystitis stays in the bladder lining; pyelonephritis reaches kidney tissue, so it brings fever and systemic illness.

checks.q: Which UTI involves the renal parenchyma?
checks.why: Pyelonephritis is parenchymal infection; cystitis is limited to bladder mucosa.

III-11.explain: Gut bacteria ascend the urethra; P fimbriae let E. coli stick to uroepithelium. Anything causing stasis or reflux raises risk.

checks.q: Most frequent pathogen in childhood UTI?
checks.why: E. coli (P fimbriae) is commonest; Klebsiella and Proteus are less frequent.

checks.q: Which is a recognised UTI risk factor in children?
checks.why: Constipation, VUR, PUV and dysfunctional voiding cause stasis and raise UTI risk.

III-11.explain: Primary VUR comes from a short ureteric tunnel in the bladder wall, so the valve fails. Kidney infection scars tissue, leading to HTN and CKD.

checks.q: What causes primary VUR?
checks.why: Primary VUR is a short intramural tunnel; PUV and neurogenic bladder cause secondary VUR.

checks.q: Long-term risk of renal scarring after pyelonephritis?
checks.why: Scarring leads to hypertension and CKD.

III-11.explain: Infants cannot localise symptoms, so UTI looks like sepsis. Older children show bladder (dysuria) or kidney (loin pain, fever) features.
III-11.hook: Febrile infant, no focus: check the urine.

checks.q: Typical infant UTI presentation?
checks.why: Infants present non-specifically: fever, vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice, sepsis.

checks.q: Which feature suggests pyelonephritis over cystitis?
checks.why: Fever and loin pain point to the kidney; dysuria/frequency to the bladder.

III-11.explain: Dipstick screens, culture confirms. WBC casts prove renal origin. MCU shows reflux; DMSA later shows permanent scars.

checks.q: Dipstick markers for UTI?
checks.why: Nitrite + leucocyte esterase on a clean/catheter sample, confirmed by culture.

checks.q: Typical urine sediment in pyelonephritis?
options: Hyaline casts and oval fat bodies
checks.why: Leucocytes, WBC casts and bacteria; RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis.

checks.q: Which test is used to diagnose VUR?
checks.why: MCU, sonocystography or dynamic scintigraphy show reflux; DMSA shows scars at 4-6 months.

III-11.explain: Young infants risk bacteraemia so need IV therapy. Pyelonephritis needs longer courses than cystitis. VUR: prevent infection, operate if breakthrough.

checks.q: UTI management in an infant under 3 months?
options: Oral cefalexin at home for 3 days
Observe and repeat urine in 48 h
checks.why: Under 3 months: admit and give IV third-generation cephalosporin.

checks.q: Oral antibiotic duration for pyelonephritis?
checks.why: Pyelonephritis 7-10 days (cefalexin/co-amoxiclav); cystitis only 3 days.

checks.q: VUR indication for surgery?
options: Any grade I reflux on MCU
checks.why: Surgery is for breakthrough infections despite prophylaxis and bowel/bladder care.

III-12.explain: Unlike adults, children's stones usually reflect an underlying metabolic disorder, so every child needs a work-up.

checks.q: Most childhood urinary stones are mainly what?
checks.why: Paediatric stones are mostly metabolic, so all children get a metabolic work-up.

III-12.explain: Too much calcium in urine is the top cause; low citrate, oxalate, cystine and RTA follow. Proteus, stasis and some drugs add risk.

checks.q: Commonest metabolic abnormality in paediatric stones?
checks.why: Hypercalciuria is commonest; hypocitraturia, hyperoxaluria, cystinuria follow.

checks.q: Which drug causes stones in preterm infants?
checks.why: Loop diuretic furosemide raises urinary calcium in preterms; topiramate also causes stones.

III-12.explain: Stones form when urine is supersaturated. Citrate binds calcium and inhibits crystals. Urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinising urine for struvite.

checks.q: Main urinary inhibitor of stone formation?
checks.why: Citrate chelates calcium; low citrate promotes supersaturation.

checks.q: Struvite stones form in which urine?
checks.why: Urease (e.g. Proteus) makes ammonia, alkalinising urine for struvite.

III-12.explain: Teenagers present like adults with colic. Young children cannot describe pain, so present vaguely or with UTI/haematuria. Cystine crystals are hexagonal.

checks.q: Classic stone pain in adolescents radiates where?
checks.why: Renal colic: flank to groin with nausea and haematuria.

checks.q: How do young children with stones often present?
checks.why: Young children are atypical: vague pain, irritability, UTI, painless haematuria.

checks.q: Hexagonal urinary crystals indicate which disorder?
checks.why: Hexagonal crystals are cystine; oxalate crystals are envelope-shaped.

III-12.explain: Ultrasound avoids radiation and is first. CT only if unclear. Metabolic work-up is mandatory in every child.

checks.q: First-line imaging for suspected stones in children?
checks.why: Ultrasound first; KUB for calcium stones; low-dose CT only if unclear.

checks.q: Who needs metabolic stone work-up?
checks.why: Every child: blood/urine calcium, oxalate, citrate, cystine, plus stone analysis.

III-12.explain: Small stones pass with analgesia and fluids. Infected obstructed kidney is an emergency. Prevention targets cause: thiazides cut urine calcium.

checks.q: Obstructed infected kidney needs what?
checks.why: An obstructed infected kidney needs urgent drainage plus antibiotics.

checks.q: Stones below which size usually pass?
checks.why: Stones <5 mm usually pass (tamsulosin helps); larger ones need ESWL/ureteroscopy/PCNL.

checks.q: Which drug reduces urinary calcium in stone prevention?
checks.why: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium; furosemide increases it.

III-13.explain: Inflamed glomeruli leak red cells (and some protein), giving the nephritic picture of haematuria, HTN and oedema.

checks.q: Hallmark urine finding in glomerulonephritis?
checks.why: GN causes haematuria ± proteinuria: the nephritic syndrome.

III-13.explain: IgA nephropathy is the most frequent GN; PSGN follows streptococcal infection. Alport is a collagen IV defect affecting kidney and ear.
III-13.hook: Alport: can't pee, can't see, can't hear.

checks.q: Most frequent glomerulonephritis type?
checks.why: IgA nephropathy is commonest; PSGN follows group A strep.

checks.q: Which is an ANCA-negative cause of GN here?
checks.why: Anti-GBM is antibody-mediated, not ANCA; the notes list lupus, MPGN, HSP, ANCA, anti-GBM.

checks.q: Haematuria with sensorineural deafness suggests?
checks.why: Alport (collagen IV) causes haematuria plus deafness and eye changes.

III-13.explain: Immune complexes damage the filter, letting RBCs and casts through. Low GFR with ongoing sodium retention causes oedema and HTN.

checks.q: What damages the GBM in most GN?
checks.why: Immune complexes break the GBM, releasing RBCs and casts.

checks.q: Why does GN cause oedema and hypertension?
checks.why: Falling GFR plus continued sodium reabsorption expands volume.

III-13.explain: Classic nephritic child: cola urine, puffy eyes, high BP. Timing after infection separates IgA (days) from PSGN (weeks).

checks.q: Classic urine colour in acute nephritis?
checks.why: Cola urine, periorbital oedema, hypertension, oliguria.

checks.q: PSGN appears how long after pharyngitis?
checks.why: PSGN: 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis, 3-6 after impetigo; IgA: 1-2 days after URTI.

III-13.explain: RBC casts prove glomerular bleeding. Complement separates PSGN (low C3, recovers by 6-8 weeks) from IgA (normal C3).
III-13.hook: Low C3 = PSGN; normal C3 = IgA.

checks.q: Typical urine in glomerulonephritis?
checks.why: RBCs with RBC casts, usually with proteinuria; WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis.

checks.q: By when does C3 normalise in PSGN?
checks.why: C3 is low in PSGN and recovers by 6-8 weeks; persistent low C3 suggests MPGN/lupus.

III-13.explain: PSGN is self-limiting: manage fluid and BP. IgA: ACE inhibitor cuts proteinuria. RPGN is urgent immunosuppression.

checks.q: Core PSGN treatment?
checks.why: PSGN is supportive: salt/fluid restriction, diuretic, antihypertensives, penicillin.

checks.q: First-line therapy for IgA nephropathy?
checks.why: ACE inhibitor reduces proteinuria; steroids for heavier disease.

checks.q: Extra treatment for anti-GBM RPGN?
checks.why: Pulse methylprednisolone, immunosuppression, plus plasma exchange for anti-GBM.

III-14.explain: Massive protein leak lowers albumin, causing oedema; the liver compensates by making more lipoproteins.
III-14.hook: Protein out, albumin down, fat up, swelling.

checks.q: Serum albumin threshold in nephrotic syndrome?
checks.why: Albumin <30 g/L with UPCR ≥200 mg/mmol, oedema and hyperlipidaemia.

III-14.explain: Most young children have steroid-sensitive minimal change disease. Atypical features suggest another lesion and prompt biopsy.

checks.q: Commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children?
checks.why: Minimal change, age 2-6, boys, ~80-90%.

checks.q: Which feature makes nephrotic syndrome atypical?
checks.why: Atypical: <1 or >12 y, HTN, macroscopic haematuria, low C3, renal impairment.

III-14.explain: Podocyte effacement lets albumin leak, dropping oncotic pressure. Losing antithrombin causes clots; losing IgG causes infections.
III-14.hook: Lose AT-III = clot; lose IgG = infect.

checks.q: What structural change underlies minimal change disease?
checks.why: A circulating factor causes podocyte foot-process effacement.

checks.q: Which urinary loss predisposes to thrombosis?
checks.why: Urinary loss of antithrombin III makes children hypercoagulable.

III-14.explain: Gravity spreads oedema: eyes in the morning, legs later. Lost IgG and ascites set up pneumococcal peritonitis.

checks.q: Where is oedema typically first noticed?
checks.why: Periorbital oedema in the morning, then legs, scrotum, ascites.

checks.q: Classic organism of peritonitis in nephrotic syndrome?
checks.why: Spontaneous peritonitis is classically pneumococcal.

III-14.explain: Confirm with UPCR, albumin, lipids. Failing 4 weeks of steroids means a different disease, so biopsy and genetics.

checks.q: Key urine test for nephrotic syndrome?
checks.why: UPCR quantifies proteinuria, with serum albumin and lipids.

checks.q: Steroid resistance is defined after how long?
checks.why: No remission after 4 weeks daily prednisolone = steroid-resistant → biopsy, genetics.

III-14.explain: Steroids induce remission in minimal change. Albumin only for symptomatic hypovolaemia. Relapsers need steroid-sparing agents.

checks.q: First-episode prednisolone regimen?
checks.why: Daily prednisolone 4 weeks then alternate days 4 weeks.

checks.q: Indication for 20% albumin?
checks.why: Albumin is reserved for symptomatic hypovolaemia; plus pneumococcal vaccine, no added salt.

checks.q: Treatment for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome?
checks.why: Resistant: calcineurin inhibitor + ACE inhibitor; relapsing: CNI, MMF, rituximab.

III-15.explain: AKI is defined by a quick creatinine rise; CKD by damage lasting over 3 months, staged by GFR.

checks.q: KDIGO AKI: creatinine rise within 48 h?
checks.why: ≥26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) in 48 h or ≥1.5× in 7 days.

checks.q: CKD G5 corresponds to GFR below?
checks.why: G5 (kidney failure) is GFR <15; CKD requires >3 months abnormality.

III-15.explain: Most paediatric AKI is from poor perfusion (dehydration). Boys' outflow obstruction is PUV. HUS follows bloody diarrhoea; CAKUT dominates CKD.

checks.q: Commonest post-renal AKI cause in boys?
checks.why: PUV is the classic post-renal cause; pre-renal is commonest overall.

checks.q: Intrinsic AKI after bloody diarrhoea suggests?
checks.why: STEC HUS follows bloody diarrhoea; CAKUT is the commonest CKD cause.

III-15.explain: Hypoperfused kidneys hold on to sodium and water (FENa<1%). Failing kidneys can't excrete K⁺. CKD loses EPO and vitamin D activation.
III-15.hook: Pre-renal: kidney is thirsty, keeps salt.

checks.q: FENa in pre-renal AKI?
checks.why: Pre-renal kidneys retain Na: FENa <1%; intrinsic AKI usually >2%.

checks.q: Most dangerous electrolyte effect of AKI?
checks.why: Lost K⁺ excretion causes hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia.

checks.q: Why is CKD associated with anaemia?
checks.why: Kidneys make erythropoietin; CKD also brings high PTH and phosphate, low calcium.

III-15.explain: AKI = fluid and toxin retention. CKD in children adds bone disease and growth failure. HUS has a classic triad.

checks.q: Typical urine output in AKI?
checks.why: Oliguria, fluid overload, hypertension, uraemia.

checks.q: CKD-specific feature in children?
checks.why: CKD: anaemia, bone disease, HTN, growth failure.

checks.q: HUS triad includes which?
checks.why: MAHA, thrombocytopenia and AKI.

III-15.explain: Creatinine and urine sodium separate pre-renal from intrinsic; US excludes obstruction. ECG shows the danger of high K⁺.

checks.q: Earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia?
checks.why: Peaked T, then wide QRS; U waves suggest hypokalaemia.

III-15.explain: Replace insensible losses plus urine output. Hyperkalaemia: stabilise membrane, shift K⁺, remove it. CKD: replace EPO, bind phosphate, transplant early.
III-15.hook: Calcium protects, insulin shifts, resin removes.

checks.q: Insensible fluid losses in AKI fluid plan?
checks.why: Give insensible 300-400 mL/m²/day plus urine output.

checks.q: First drug in hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?
checks.why: Calcium gluconate stabilises myocardium first, then shift (salbutamol/insulin), then remove.

checks.q: Treatment for atypical HUS?
checks.why: Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS responds to eculizumab.

III-16.explain: CAKUT covers all structural kidney/tract malformations and causes most childhood CKD.

checks.q: Commonest cause of childhood CKD?
checks.why: CAKUT is the leading cause of paediatric CKD.

III-16.explain: Kidney forms when ureteric bud meets mesenchyme; failure gives agenesis or dysplasia. Duplex upper ureter obstructs, lower refluxes.

checks.q: Horseshoe kidney results from what?
checks.why: Fused lower poles get stuck during ascent; failed induction gives agenesis/dysplasia.

checks.q: In a duplex kidney, which ureter refluxes?
checks.why: Lower-pole ureter refluxes; the upper-pole ureter (often ectopic/ureterocele) obstructs.

III-16.explain: No kidneys means no fetal urine, oligohydramnios, and lungs that can't develop. Obstruction damages the developing kidney.
III-16.hook: No urine, no fluid, no lungs.

checks.q: Bilateral renal agenesis leads to which sequence?
checks.why: Oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia and compression features: Potter sequence.

checks.q: PUV causes renal damage by what?
checks.why: Outflow obstruction raises pressure, causing dysplasia and CKD.

checks.q: VUR leads to CKD mainly via?
checks.why: Reflux → pyelonephritis → focal scars → HTN, CKD.

III-16.explain: Dilated pelvis with normal ureter points to PUJ. Boys with poor stream and big bladder: PUV. VUR runs in families.

checks.q: Commonest cause of antenatal hydronephrosis (normal ureter)?
checks.why: PUJ obstruction dilates the pelvis but not the ureter.

checks.q: Classic sign of PUV in a boy?
checks.why: Poor stream, palpable bladder, UTI; commonest lower tract obstruction in boys.

checks.q: Sibling risk of VUR?
checks.why: Siblings of VUR children have ~30% risk.

III-16.explain: Newborns are relatively dehydrated so early US underestimates dilatation. MCUG grades reflux; MAG3 assesses drainage; DMSA scars.
III-16.hook: MCUG grades, MAG3 drains, DMSA scars.

checks.q: Why delay postnatal US beyond first days?
options: Kidneys are too small to image
checks.why: Neonatal low urine output underestimates dilatation in the first days.

checks.q: Test to diagnose and grade VUR?
checks.why: MCUG grades VUR I-V; MAG3 for drainage; DMSA for scars.

III-16.explain: PUJ: operate only if function falls. PUV is an emergency needing drainage then valve ablation. VUR: prevent infection, reimplant if breakthrough.

checks.q: PUJ obstruction operation indication?
checks.why: Pyeloplasty if split function falls.

checks.q: Immediate management of PUV?
checks.why: Urgent catheter drainage, then endoscopic valve ablation.

checks.q: VUR indication for ureteric reimplantation?
checks.why: Reimplantation for breakthrough infection; prophylaxis if high grade.

III-17.explain: Each tubulopathy maps to the segment whose transporter fails, which predicts its electrolyte pattern.
III-17.hook: Know the segment, know the syndrome.

checks.q: Renal tubulopathies are classically classified by what?
checks.why: Inherited transporter defects are mapped to nephron segments.

III-17.explain: Proximal = Fanconi (cystinosis), loop = Bartter, DCT = Gitelman, collecting duct = RTA and nephrogenic DI.
III-17.hook: Bartter = loop (B before G, loop before DCT).

checks.q: Commonest cause of Fanconi syndrome in children?
checks.why: Cystinosis is the commonest paediatric cause of Fanconi syndrome.

checks.q: Gene in X-linked nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: X-linked nephrogenic DI is AVPR2 (vasopressin receptor 2); AQP2 is AR.

III-17.explain: Salt wasting triggers renin-aldosterone, which dumps K⁺ and H⁺. Distal RTA can't secrete acid, so urine pH stays high and calcium deposits.
III-17.hook: Distal RTA: urine pH >5.5 despite acidosis.

checks.q: Acid-base disturbance in Bartter/Gitelman?
checks.why: Salt wasting raises aldosterone → hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

checks.q: Urine pH in distal RTA during acidosis?
checks.why: No H⁺ secretion: urine pH stays >5.5 despite normal-gap acidosis.

III-17.explain: Fanconi wastes glucose and phosphate. Bartter acts like furosemide (high urine Ca); Gitelman like thiazides (low urine Ca, low Mg).

checks.q: Glycosuria with normal blood glucose suggests?
checks.why: Fanconi (proximal) wastes glucose and phosphate → rickets, FTT.

checks.q: Which tubulopathy causes polyhydramnios and nephrocalcinosis?
checks.why: Bartter mimics furosemide: hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, polyhydramnios.

checks.q: Gitelman is characterised by which?
checks.why: Gitelman mimics thiazides: low Mg, low urinary Ca, cramps, tetany.

III-17.explain: Gas, K, Mg, urine pH and calcium sort the syndromes. Cystinosis deposits crystals in the cornea. Nephrogenic DI ignores desmopressin.

checks.q: Eye finding in cystinosis?
checks.why: Cystine crystals deposit in the cornea.

checks.q: Desmopressin response in nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: Nephrogenic DI: dilute urine, hypernatraemia, no response to desmopressin.

III-17.explain: Cysteamine depletes cystine. Replace what is lost. Indometacin blocks prostaglandin excess in Bartter. Thiazide paradoxically cuts urine volume in DI.

checks.q: Specific treatment for cystinosis?
checks.why: Cysteamine depletes lysosomal cystine; tiopronin is for cystinuria stones.

checks.q: Specific drug used in Bartter syndrome?
checks.why: Indometacin + K for Bartter; Gitelman needs Mg + K.

checks.q: Distal RTA treatment?
checks.why: Alkali (citrate) for distal RTA; free water + thiazide for nephrogenic DI.

III-18.explain: Chromosome disorders are either wrong number (trisomy, monosomy) or wrong structure (deletions, translocations).

checks.q: Turner 45,X is which type of error?
checks.why: Turner is a numerical sex chromosome aneuploidy.

III-18.explain: Most Down syndrome is maternal non-disjunction; translocation cases may be inherited, so karyotype parents. Know the named deletions.

checks.q: Commonest mechanism of Down syndrome?
checks.why: ~95% non-disjunction (maternal age); ~4% translocation; ~1% mosaic.

checks.q: Williams syndrome deletion?
checks.why: Williams = 7q11.23; DiGeorge = 22q11; Prader-Willi/Angelman = 15q11-13.

III-18.explain: Chromosome 21 carries APP, so extra copies cause early Alzheimer. Third/fourth pharyngeal pouch loss in 22q11 removes thymus and parathyroids.

checks.q: Classic Down syndrome heart defect?
checks.why: Endocardial cushion defect → AVSD.

checks.q: Hypocalcaemia in 22q11 deletion is due to?
checks.why: Parathyroid hypoplasia; thymic hypoplasia causes infections.

checks.q: Gene causing short stature in Turner?
checks.why: SHOX haploinsufficiency; FGFR3 is achondroplasia.

III-18.explain: Down: hypotonia plus GI, blood and thyroid problems. Edwards = clenched fists; Patau = midline defects. Turner = coarctation; Klinefelter = tall, small testes.

checks.q: GI atresia classically linked to trisomy 21?
checks.why: Duodenal atresia (double bubble) is the classic Down association.

checks.q: Clenched fists with overlapping fingers suggest?
checks.why: Edwards (T18); Patau has holoprosencephaly, cleft lip, polydactyly.

checks.q: Cardiac lesion typical of Turner syndrome?
checks.why: Turner: coarctation, bicuspid valve; 22q11: conotruncal defects.

III-18.explain: Screening (combined test, NIPT) gives risk; invasive tests (CVS/amnio) diagnose. Microdeletions are too small for karyotype, so microarray/FISH.

checks.q: Diagnostic follow-up after high-risk NIPT?
checks.why: NIPT is screening; CVS/amniocentesis with QF-PCR/karyotype confirms.

checks.q: Best test for microdeletions?
checks.why: Microdeletions need microarray or FISH; karyotype parents in translocation Down.

III-18.explain: Down care is lifelong screening for predictable problems. Turner: GH and oestrogen; Y material risks gonadoblastoma. Klinefelter: testosterone at puberty.

checks.q: Which is routinely screened in Down syndrome?
checks.why: Heart, thyroid, hearing, eyes, coeliac.

checks.q: Why check for Y material in Turner?
checks.why: Y material raises gonadoblastoma risk; GH + oestrogen are standard treatment.

checks.q: Treatment for Klinefelter at puberty?
checks.why: Testosterone replacement from puberty.

III-19.explain: Dominant disease shows with one faulty copy; recessive needs both copies faulty, so carriers are well.

checks.q: How many mutant alleles cause AR disease?
checks.why: AR needs both alleles mutated; AD needs one.

III-19.explain: Structural proteins and receptors (fibrillin, FGFR3) tend to be AD; enzymes and channels (CF, PKU) tend to be AR.

checks.q: Achondroplasia mechanism?
checks.why: Achondroplasia is AD FGFR3 gain-of-function; Marfan is fibrillin-1.

checks.q: SMA is caused by deletion of which gene?
checks.why: SMA is AR SMN1 deletion; SMN2 copies modify severity.

III-19.explain: AD works via haploinsufficiency, dominant negative or gain of function, often de novo with older fathers. Half enzyme activity suffices, so enzyme defects are AR.

checks.q: De novo AD mutations are linked to what?
checks.why: Advanced paternal age increases de novo AD point mutations.

checks.q: Why are most enzyme deficiencies AR?
checks.why: Carriers with 50% activity are healthy, so disease needs both alleles.

III-19.explain: AD pedigrees are vertical with male-to-male transmission; AR horizontal with 25% risk. Healthy siblings of AR child: 2/3 carriers.

checks.q: Which pedigree feature excludes X-linked inheritance?
checks.why: Male-to-male transmission occurs in AD but not X-linked.

checks.q: Recurrence risk for AR when both parents carry?
checks.why: Two carriers: 25% per pregnancy.

checks.q: Carrier probability of healthy sibling of AR child?
checks.why: Excluding the affected genotype leaves 2 of 3 carriers.

III-19.explain: Sequencing identifies the mutation; prenatal and newborn screening catch treatable AR diseases early.

checks.q: Broadest genetic test for undiagnosed Mendelian disease?
checks.why: Exome/genome sequencing covers single-gene disorders broadly.

checks.q: Which is on newborn screening?
checks.why: Newborn screening includes PKU, CAH, galactosaemia, CF, SMA.

III-19.explain: Counselling is non-directive: give risks, let families decide. Test relatives once a mutation is known; some diseases now have targeted therapy.

checks.q: Genetic counselling style should be?
checks.why: Non-directive counselling with risk calculation.

checks.q: Disease-specific therapy for SMA?
checks.why: Nusinersen (antisense to SMN2); cascade testing of relatives follows.

III-20.explain: XLR shows in boys via carrier mothers; fathers can't pass X to sons. XLD affected fathers give X to every daughter.

checks.q: Which is excluded in X-linked recessive inheritance?
checks.why: Fathers give Y to sons, so no male-to-male transmission.

checks.q: In XLD, an affected father's daughters are?
checks.why: He passes his X to all daughters, so all are affected.

III-20.explain: Carrier mother gives each son 50% risk. Affected father makes all daughters carriers. Duchenne has many new mutations (~1/3).

checks.q: Risk each son of a carrier mother is affected?
checks.why: Each son has 50% chance of inheriting the mutant X.

checks.q: Proportion of Duchenne cases from new mutations?
checks.why: About one-third of DMD cases are de novo.

III-20.explain: Males have one X so show disease. Random X-inactivation protects carriers. Frame-shift kills dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame keeps some (Becker).
III-20.hook: Out of frame = Duchenne; in frame = Becker.

checks.q: What usually protects female carriers?
checks.why: Random X-inactivation leaves most carriers with enough normal protein.

checks.q: Duchenne dystrophin deletion is typically?
checks.why: Out-of-frame deletion → no dystrophin; Becker is in-frame.

checks.q: Gene mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia?
checks.why: XLA = BTK; fragile X = FMR1 CGG repeat.

III-20.explain: DMD: proximal weakness by 2-5 with Gowers sign. XLA infections start once maternal IgG wanes (~6 months). WAS triad: eczema, small platelets, infections.

checks.q: Typical age of DMD presentation?
checks.why: Age 2-5: Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, falls.

checks.q: When do XLA infections typically start?
checks.why: Maternal IgG protects until ~6 months.

checks.q: Platelets in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome are?
checks.why: WAS: thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, infections.

III-20.explain: Muscle breakdown makes CK huge in DMD. Haemophilia affects intrinsic pathway: isolated long APTT.

checks.q: First test in suspected Duchenne?
checks.why: CK (>10 000 U/L), then genetic testing.

checks.q: Coagulation profile in haemophilia?
checks.why: Isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets.

III-20.explain: Steroids slow DMD. Suxamethonium can cause hyperkalaemia/rhabdo in myopathy. Haemophilia: no IM or NSAIDs. XLA: no live vaccines.

checks.q: Disease-slowing drug class in DMD?
checks.why: Prednisolone or deflazacort plus physio and cardiorespiratory surveillance.

checks.q: Which anaesthetic drug is avoided in DMD?
checks.why: Suxamethonium risks hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis in DMD.

checks.q: Which vaccines are contraindicated in XLA?
checks.why: No B cells: live vaccines can cause disease.

III-21.explain: Many small genetic effects plus environment add up; disease appears only once total liability crosses a threshold.

checks.q: Multifactorial disease appears when liability does what?
checks.why: Combined genetic + environmental liability must exceed a threshold.

III-21.explain: Some conditions favour boys (pyloric stenosis, cleft lip), others girls (DDH, cleft palate, NTDs).

checks.q: Pyloric stenosis is how much commoner in boys?
checks.why: About 4-5 times commoner in boys.

checks.q: Which multifactorial disorder is commoner in girls?
checks.why: DDH, isolated cleft palate and NTDs favour girls.

III-21.explain: Relatives share genes, so their liability curve sits nearer the threshold. An affected rarer sex carries more liability (Carter effect).

checks.q: Recurrence risks in multifactorial disease are?
checks.why: Recurrence is empiric, derived from population data.

checks.q: Carter effect: higher risk when affected proband is?
options: The commoner sex for that disorder
An only child of healthy parents
checks.why: Affected less common sex implies higher liability, so relatives have more risk.

III-21.explain: Risk to first-degree relatives is a few percent and drops fast with distance. Severity, multiple affected and rare sex raise it.

checks.q: First-degree recurrence risk for an isolated malformation?
checks.why: About 2-5%, falling sharply in second-degree relatives.

checks.q: Which increases multifactorial recurrence risk?
checks.why: Severity, ≥2 affected relatives and affected rarer sex raise risk.

III-21.explain: Extra anomalies suggest a syndrome with different (often higher) risk. Open NTDs leak AFP into maternal blood.

checks.q: Malformation plus dysmorphism: first step?
checks.why: Exclude syndromes (22q11, trisomy 13) first.

checks.q: Maternal serum marker for NTD screening?
checks.why: Raised AFP plus anomaly ultrasound.

III-21.explain: Folic acid preconception sharply cuts NTDs. Higher dose for high-risk women; the US uses 4 mg after a previous NTD.

checks.q: NTD recurrence risk without folate?
checks.why: About 3-5% after an affected pregnancy without folate.

checks.q: Folic acid dose for a high-risk woman?
checks.why: High-risk: 5 mg daily; everyone else: 400 µg, preconception to 12 weeks.

checks.q: US folic acid dose after a previous NTD pregnancy?
checks.why: US guidance: 4 mg daily after a prior NTD pregnancy.

III-22.explain: Enzyme defects are mostly AR because carriers' 50% enzyme activity suffices.

checks.q: Typical inheritance of amino acid disorders?
checks.why: Mostly AR enzyme defects.

III-22.explain: Each disorder blocks one enzyme: PKU (phenylalanine hydroxylase), MSUD (BCKD), tyrosinaemia 1 (FAH), homocystinuria (CBS).

checks.q: Enzyme deficient in classic PKU?
checks.why: PKU = phenylalanine hydroxylase; MSUD = branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.

checks.q: Enzyme deficient in homocystinuria?
checks.why: Homocystinuria = CBS; tyrosinaemia 1 = FAH.

III-22.explain: The placenta clears toxins in utero, so babies are well until protein feeds. PKU lowers tyrosine and thus melanin; leucine in MSUD swells the brain.
III-22.hook: Well at birth, sick after milk.

checks.q: Why are newborns with aminoacidopathies well at birth?
checks.why: The placenta removes toxic metabolites before birth.

checks.q: Why do PKU children have fair hair?
checks.why: Tyrosine is the melanin precursor and is low in PKU.

III-22.explain: Metabolic crises mimic sepsis. Smells help: musty (PKU), maple syrup (MSUD). Homocystinuria lens dislocates down, Marfan up.

checks.q: Neonatal metabolic crisis typically mimics?
checks.why: Poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma: sepsis-like.

checks.q: Sweet-smelling urine with neonatal encephalopathy?
checks.why: MSUD smells sweet; untreated PKU smells musty.

checks.q: Lens dislocation direction in homocystinuria?
checks.why: Downwards (inferonasal) in homocystinuria; upwards in Marfan.

III-22.explain: PKU is caught on newborn heel prick. In crisis, a basic metabolic screen includes ammonia and urine organic acids.
III-22.hook: Crisis bloods: glucose, gas, lactate, ammonia.

checks.q: How is PKU diagnosed?
options: Urine ferric chloride test in infancy
checks.why: Newborn blood-spot phenylalanine screening.

checks.q: Which is a key crisis investigation?
checks.why: Glucose, gas, lactate, ammonia, amino acids, urine organic acids.

III-22.explain: Stop protein and give glucose to halt catabolism. Remove ammonia; then disease-specific diets/drugs.

checks.q: First step in acute metabolic crisis?
checks.why: Stop protein and give high-energy IV glucose to stop catabolism.

checks.q: PKU long-term management?
checks.why: Lifelong low-phenylalanine diet ± sapropterin.

checks.q: Specific drug for tyrosinaemia type 1?
checks.why: Nitisinone; pyridoxine for homocystinuria.

III-23.explain: These are inherited blocks in handling glycogen, galactose or fructose, causing hypoglycaemia, liver or muscle disease.

checks.q: Galactosaemia belongs to which group?
checks.why: Glycogen, galactose and fructose defects form this group.

III-23.explain: Von Gierke lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so the liver can't release glucose. Each named disease has a classic enzyme.

checks.q: Enzyme deficient in von Gierke disease?
checks.why: GSD I = glucose-6-phosphatase; Pompe = acid maltase; McArdle = myophosphorylase.

checks.q: Enzyme deficient in hereditary fructose intolerance?
checks.why: Aldolase B; galactosaemia = GALT.

III-23.explain: Trapped G6P is shunted to lactate, urate and fat. MCAD can't burn fat, so fasting gives hypoglycaemia without ketones.

checks.q: Which rises in von Gierke disease?
checks.why: G6P is diverted: lactate, uric acid and triglycerides rise.

checks.q: Hypoglycaemia type in MCAD deficiency?
checks.why: Fat oxidation fails, so no ketones: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

III-23.explain: Hepatomegaly + hypoglycaemia (afebrile) = von Gierke. Pompe affects heart; McArdle muscle. Galactosaemia appears on milk; HFI at weaning.

checks.q: Afebrile infant, hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly suggests?
checks.why: Classic GSD type I (von Gierke).

checks.q: Pompe disease classically causes which?
checks.why: Pompe: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and hypotonia; McArdle: cramps, second wind.

checks.q: Classic sepsis organism in galactosaemia?
checks.why: Galactosaemic neonates are prone to E. coli sepsis.

III-23.explain: Von Gierke hypoglycaemia comes quickly after feeds. Galactosaemia: low GALT and urine reducing substances. McArdle muscle breakdown raises CK.
III-23.hook: Hypo 2-4 h after feed = GSD I.

checks.q: Fasting tolerance in GSD I?
checks.why: Hypoglycaemia 2-4 h after feeds, with lactic acidosis and high urate.

checks.q: Diagnostic test for galactosaemia?
checks.why: Red-cell GALT plus urine reducing substances; CK is for McArdle.

III-23.explain: GSD I needs constant glucose supply (cornstarch). Pompe gets ERT. Galactosaemia: stop lactose immediately. Avoid fasting in MCAD.
III-23.hook: Cornstarch keeps GSD I going overnight.

checks.q: Overnight treatment in GSD I?
checks.why: Frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch; allopurinol for urate.

checks.q: Immediate action in suspected galactosaemia?
checks.why: Stop lactose now, switch to soy formula.

checks.q: Key rule in MCAD deficiency?
checks.why: Avoid fasting; HFI needs fructose, sucrose, sorbitol exclusion.

III-24.explain: Missing lysosomal enzymes let substrate build up, hitting cells with high turnover such as macrophages.

checks.q: Lysosomal storage diseases are caused by?
checks.why: Enzyme deficiency → substrate accumulates in cells.

III-24.explain: Almost all are AR except Fabry and Hunter (X-linked). Each named disease has a classic enzyme.

checks.q: Which lysosomal disease is X-linked?
checks.why: Hunter and Fabry are X-linked; the rest are mostly AR.

checks.q: Enzyme deficient in Gaucher disease?
checks.why: Gaucher = β-glucocerebrosidase; Tay-Sachs = hex A; Hurler = α-L-iduronidase.

III-24.explain: Storage in macrophages enlarges liver/spleen; in neurons causes regression and cherry-red spot; in connective tissue (GAGs) coarsens the face.

checks.q: Macrophage storage typically causes?
checks.why: Macrophage storage → hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias.

checks.q: GAG storage (MPS) typically causes which?
checks.why: GAGs: coarse face, dysostosis multiplex, valve disease, corneal clouding.

III-24.explain: Babies seem normal, then regress. Cherry-red spot: Tay-Sachs (no organomegaly) vs Niemann-Pick (organomegaly). Hurler clouds corneas, Hunter doesn't.

checks.q: Key alarm feature of lysosomal disease?
checks.why: Normal at birth then regression.

checks.q: Cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly?
checks.why: Tay-Sachs; with hepatosplenomegaly think Niemann-Pick.

checks.q: Burning pain in hands/feet suggests?
checks.why: Fabry causes acroparaesthesia; Gaucher bone crises; Hurler corneal clouding.

III-24.explain: Enzyme assay in leucocytes or dried blood spots confirms. Urine GAGs screen MPS; some are on newborn screening.

checks.q: Confirmatory test for lysosomal disease?
checks.why: Enzyme activity in leucocytes or dried blood spots.

checks.q: Which lysosomal disease is newborn screened?
checks.why: Newborn screening covers Pompe and MPS I.

III-24.explain: ERT is a large protein that can't cross the blood-brain barrier. HSCT in Hurler before ~2 years provides enzyme to the brain.
III-24.hook: ERT can't get into the brain.

checks.q: Why does ERT not treat CNS disease?
checks.why: ERT does not cross the BBB.

checks.q: Which disease is treated with ERT?
checks.why: Gaucher, Fabry, Hunter: ERT or substrate reduction.

checks.q: HSCT preserves cognition in Hurler if done before?
checks.why: HSCT before ~2 years preserves cognition.

III-25.explain: Upper airway inflammation spans the nose (rhinitis), adenoids and tonsils, all lymphoid-rich in childhood.

checks.q: Adenoid enlargement is best described as?
checks.why: Adenoid hypertrophy, alongside rhinitis and tonsillitis.

III-25.explain: Rhinitis is viral or IgE-allergic. Most sore throats are viral; GAS is the leading bacterial cause in school-age children.

checks.q: Mechanism of allergic rhinitis?
checks.why: Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated; otherwise viral.

checks.q: Peak age for group A strep tonsillitis?
checks.why: GAS is the commonest bacterial cause at 5-15 years.

III-25.explain: Big adenoids block the nose and Eustachian tubes, causing snoring, OSA and otitis. GAS can trigger rheumatic fever and PSGN.

checks.q: Peak age of adenoid hypertrophy?
checks.why: Adenoids peak at 3-7 years, blocking nose and Eustachian tubes.

checks.q: PSGN follows pharyngitis by how long?
checks.why: About 1-2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis (notes; elsewhere quoted 1-3 weeks).

III-25.explain: Itch and sneeze = allergy. Unilateral smelly discharge in a toddler = foreign body. Centor-type features suggest GAS; quinsy shows trismus and uvular deviation.

checks.q: Unilateral foul nasal discharge in a toddler suggests?
checks.why: Unilateral foul discharge = foreign body until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Which favours GAS over viral pharyngitis?
checks.why: Fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough.

checks.q: Trismus, hot-potato voice, deviated uvula suggest?
checks.why: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess).

III-25.explain: Rapid antigen tests miss some GAS, so a negative test is backed by culture. Adenoids are seen on nasendoscopy or lateral X-ray.

checks.q: Next step after negative rapid strep test?
checks.why: Low sensitivity, so a negative antigen test is backed by throat culture.

checks.q: Imaging for adenoid size?
checks.why: Nasendoscopy or lateral neck X-ray; sleep study if OSA uncertain.

III-25.explain: Intranasal steroids are best for allergic rhinitis. Penicillin for 10 days prevents rheumatic fever (not PSGN); amoxicillin in EBV causes rash.

checks.q: Most effective treatment for allergic rhinitis?
checks.why: Intranasal steroids are the most effective.

checks.q: Duration of penicillin V for GAS tonsillitis?
checks.why: 10 days prevents rheumatic fever (not PSGN).

checks.q: Indication for adenectomy?
checks.why: Recurrent URTIs, otitis media, blocked nasal breathing, OSA.
